subject: physics

items.q: Which statement best describes the internal energy of a system?
items.correct: The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all its particles
items.misconception: The total kinetic energy of all the particles moving inside it
items.why: Particle diagrams and animations show motion and nothing else, so the positions of particles relative to one another look like a fact about arrangement rather than a store of energy. The specification defines internal energy as the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles. The potential part matters: it is why energy can be supplied during melting or boiling without the particles speeding up.
items.random_wrong: The temperature that the particles inside the system have reached

items.q: Which pair of quantities are added together to give the internal energy of a system?
items.correct: The kinetic energy and the potential energy of every particle present
items.misconception: The kinetic energy of every particle and the volume of the whole system
items.why: Particle diagrams and animations show motion and nothing else, so the positions of particles relative to one another look like a fact about arrangement rather than a store of energy. The specification defines internal energy as the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles. The potential part matters: it is why energy can be supplied during melting or boiling without the particles speeding up.
items.random_wrong: The heat contained in the system and the temperature it has reached

items.q: A beaker of pure ice at 0 °C is heated steadily by an immersion heater. What happens to the energy supplied while the ice melts?
items.correct: It increases the energy of the particles and melts the ice at 0 °C
items.misconception: It increases the energy of the particles and warms the ice above 0 °C
items.why: In almost every everyday experience of heating, from a kettle to a radiator, the temperature does rise, and the thermometer is the visible sign that heating is working. Heating increases the energy of the particles. That energy can raise the temperature, or it can change the state of the substance. While ice at 0 °C is melting, the thermometer stays at 0 °C even though energy is being supplied the whole time.
items.random_wrong: It raises the temperature slowly while the ice is turning into water

items.q: Heating changes the energy stored within a system. How does it do this?
items.correct: By increasing the energy of the particles that make up the system
items.misconception: By adding a quantity of heat that the system then contains inside it
items.why: Everyday speech treats heat as a substance ('let the heat out', 'the heat in the room'), and a thermometer reading is the only number most students ever see attached to a hot object. The store held inside a system is internal energy, not heat. Heating is the transfer that changes that store. Two objects at the same temperature can hold very different internal energies, because internal energy also depends on how much substance is there.
items.random_wrong: By increasing only the potential energy of the particles already present

items.q: Beaker A holds 1 kg of a liquid and beaker B holds 2 kg of the same liquid, both starting at 20 °C. Each is given 8400 J. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: Beaker A rises by twice as many degrees as beaker B
items.misconception: Beaker B rises by twice as many degrees as beaker A does
items.why: Students confuse how much energy a sample can store with how far its temperature moves, and 'more mass, more energy' feels like the obvious rule. In ∆E = m c ∆θ, for a fixed ∆E a larger m gives a smaller ∆θ. A larger mass needs more energy for the same temperature rise, so with equal energy inputs it rises less.
items.random_wrong: Both beakers rise by the same number of degrees Celsius

items.q: Equal masses of copper and of water are each given 5000 J of energy. The temperature of the copper rises much more than that of the water. Why?
items.correct: The temperature increase depends on the type of material as well
items.misconception: Copper has the larger specific heat capacity, so it warms up faster
items.why: The word 'capacity' suggests a large container that fills readily, and 'high' is read as 'good at heating up'. Specific heat capacity is the energy required per kilogram per degree Celsius. Water, with about 4200 J/kg °C, needs far more energy per degree than copper, so for the same mass and energy input water's temperature rises far less.
items.random_wrong: Copper must have been given more energy than the water was given

items.q: Which equation gives the change in thermal energy of a substance whose temperature changes?
items.correct: ∆E = m c ∆θ
items.misconception: ∆E = m L ∆θ
items.why: The thermal energy equation is met first and contains three quantities, so students expect the latent heat calculation to look the same and hunt for a temperature to put in. The specification gives energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat, E = m L. There is no ∆θ term because the specific latent heat is defined with no change in temperature.
items.random_wrong: ∆E = m ∆θ / c

items.q: What is the unit of specific heat capacity?
items.correct: J/kg °C
items.misconception: J/kg
items.why: The two quantities have similar names, appear on the same page, and both begin 'the amount of energy required to ... one kilogram of the substance'. Specific heat capacity is per kilogram and per degree Celsius, so J/kg °C. Specific latent heat involves no change in temperature at all, so there is no degree Celsius in its unit: J/kg.
items.random_wrong: J/°C

items.q: 2.0 kg of water is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C. How much energy is transferred to the water?
items.why: The final temperature is the number the question makes most prominent, and the symbol θ looks like 'temperature' rather than 'change in temperature'. The quantity in the equation is temperature change, ∆θ, in degrees Celsius. The ∆ means 'change in', so subtract the starting temperature from the final temperature before substituting.

items.q: A 0.50 kg metal block is given 9200 J of energy and its temperature rises by 40 °C. What is the specific heat capacity of the metal, in J/kg °C?
items.why: The 'per kilogram' part of the unit is dropped when the value is read aloud, and students think of the number as belonging to the object in front of them. Specific heat capacity is defined per kilogram. For a 2 kg sample of water it would take 8400 J for each degree Celsius, and for 0.5 kg only 2100 J. That is why mass appears in ∆E = m c ∆θ.

items.q: 0.30 kg of oil at 15 °C is given 12 000 J of energy. The specific heat capacity of the oil is 2000 J/kg °C. What is the final temperature of the oil?
items.why: The final temperature is the number the question makes most prominent, and the symbol θ looks like 'temperature' rather than 'change in temperature'. The quantity in the equation is temperature change, ∆θ, in degrees Celsius. The ∆ means 'change in', so subtract the starting temperature from the final temperature before substituting.

items.q: A substance has a specific heat capacity of 900 J/kg °C. What does this tell you?
items.correct: 900 J raises the temperature of one kilogram of it by 1 °C
items.misconception: 900 J raises the temperature of the whole substance by 1 °C
items.why: The 'per kilogram' part of the unit is dropped when the value is read aloud, and students think of the number as belonging to the object in front of them. Specific heat capacity is defined per kilogram. For a 2 kg sample of water it would take 8400 J for each degree Celsius, and for 0.5 kg only 2100 J. That is why mass appears in ∆E = m c ∆θ.
items.random_wrong: 900 J changes the state of one kilogram of it without warming

items.q: Ice at 0 °C is melting while energy is supplied to it steadily. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The internal energy increases but the temperature stays at 0 °C
items.misconception: Both the internal energy and the temperature of the ice increase
items.why: Students reason that energy is still going in, so the thermometer must still be creeping up, and a flat line on a graph is read as a shallow slope. During a change of state the energy supplied changes the energy stored (internal energy) but not the temperature. The graph is genuinely flat, not gently rising, for as long as the change of state lasts.
items.random_wrong: Neither of them changes, since the temperature reading stays fixed

items.q: What is meant by the specific latent heat of a substance?
items.correct: The energy required to change the state of one kilogram with no temperature change
items.misconception: The energy required to raise the temperature of one kilogram by one degree
items.why: Both are 'specific' quantities, both are defined for one kilogram, and both appear in short equations that look alike, so they blur together in revision. Specific heat capacity applies when the temperature changes and no state change occurs. Specific latent heat applies when the state changes and the temperature does not. Deciding which is happening comes first; choosing the equation follows from that.
items.random_wrong: The energy required to change the state of one kilogram by one degree

items.q: A solid at its melting point has a specific latent heat of fusion of 250 000 J/kg. How much energy is needed to melt 200 g of it completely?
items.why: Masses in the laboratory are read off a balance in grams, and the equation is copied down without checking the unit list printed underneath it. The specification states mass, m, in kilograms, kg, for both ∆E = m c ∆θ and E = m L. Convert grams to kilograms by dividing by 1000 before substituting, or the answer is out by a factor of 1000.

items.q: 0.25 kg of a liquid at its boiling point is completely turned to vapour by 575 000 J of energy. What is its specific latent heat of vaporisation, in J/kg?
items.why: The thermal energy equation is met first and contains three quantities, so students expect the latent heat calculation to look the same and hunt for a temperature to put in. The specification gives energy for a change of state = mass × specific latent heat, E = m L. There is no ∆θ term because the specific latent heat is defined with no change in temperature.

items.q: What is the unit of specific latent heat?
items.correct: J/kg
items.misconception: J/kg °C
items.why: The two quantities have similar names, appear on the same page, and both begin 'the amount of energy required to ... one kilogram of the substance'. Specific heat capacity is per kilogram and per degree Celsius, so J/kg °C. Specific latent heat involves no change in temperature at all, so there is no degree Celsius in its unit: J/kg.
items.random_wrong: J

items.q: The specific latent heat of fusion is defined for which change of state?
items.correct: From solid to liquid
items.misconception: From liquid to vapour
items.why: 'Fusion' sounds like joining or melting together and is not everyday language, so the two terms are memorised as labels without being attached to particular changes of state. Specific latent heat of fusion is the change of state from solid to liquid. Specific latent heat of vaporisation is the change of state from liquid to vapour. They are different quantities with different values for the same substance.
items.random_wrong: From vapour to liquid

items.q: Water in a kettle is at 100 °C and is boiling away to steam. Which quantity is needed to calculate the energy transferred while it boils away?
items.correct: The specific latent heat of vaporisation of water
items.misconception: The specific latent heat of fusion of the water
items.why: 'Fusion' sounds like joining or melting together and is not everyday language, so the two terms are memorised as labels without being attached to particular changes of state. Specific latent heat of fusion is the change of state from solid to liquid. Specific latent heat of vaporisation is the change of state from liquid to vapour. They are different quantities with different values for the same substance.
items.random_wrong: The specific heat capacity of the water used

items.q: A solid is heated steadily from below its melting point until it has all boiled away. Its temperature–time graph has two flat sections. What is happening during the first, lower flat section?
items.correct: The substance is melting, so the energy raises its internal energy
items.misconception: The substance is boiling, since boiling always begins before melting
items.why: Boiling is the more familiar and more dramatic change, so it is assumed to come first, and students do not read the temperature axis to check which plateau is lower. A substance heated from solid melts before it boils, so on a heating graph the lower plateau is the melting point and the upper plateau is the boiling point. Read the temperature at each flat section to identify it.
items.random_wrong: No energy is being transferred to the substance during that time

items.q: A hot liquid is left to cool. Its temperature–time graph falls, then stays flat for several minutes, then falls again. What does the flat part show?
items.correct: The liquid is freezing, and energy is still leaving it
items.misconception: The liquid has stopped losing energy to its surroundings
items.why: Temperature is treated as the visible evidence of energy transfer, so a flat line reads as 'nothing happening' or 'the heater has been switched off'. Energy is supplied at the same steady rate throughout the flat section. It changes the internal energy of the substance as it changes state instead of raising the temperature, which is exactly why the section is flat.
items.random_wrong: The liquid has cooled to the temperature of the room

items.q: How does specific heat capacity differ from specific latent heat?
items.correct: One is for a temperature change, the other for a change of state
items.misconception: They are the same quantity, simply given two different names
items.why: Both are 'specific' quantities, both are defined for one kilogram, and both appear in short equations that look alike, so they blur together in revision. Specific heat capacity applies when the temperature changes and no state change occurs. Specific latent heat applies when the state changes and the temperature does not. Deciding which is happening comes first; choosing the equation follows from that.
items.random_wrong: One is measured per kilogram, the other for the whole sample

items.q: 500 g of aluminium is heated and its temperature rises by 20 °C. The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J/kg °C. How much energy is transferred to the aluminium?
items.why: Masses in the laboratory are read off a balance in grams, and the equation is copied down without checking the unit list printed underneath it. The specification states mass, m, in kilograms, kg, for both ∆E = m c ∆θ and E = m L. Convert grams to kilograms by dividing by 1000 before substituting, or the answer is out by a factor of 1000.

items.q: Equal masses of copper and water are given equal energy. Do they reach the same temperature rise?
items.correct: No. The temperature increase also depends on the type of material.
items.misconception: Equal energy into equal masses must give equal temperature rises.
items.why: Students remember that temperature rise depends on mass and energy input and stop there, dropping the third factor the specification lists. The increase in temperature depends on the mass of the substance heated, the type of material and the energy input. The material enters the calculation through its specific heat capacity, so copper warms far more than water for the same energy per kilogram.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: A cooling graph flattens out for several minutes. What does that show?
items.correct: The substance is changing state, and energy is still leaving it.
items.misconception: The substance has cooled all the way down to room temperature, which is why the line has gone flat.
items.why: Cooling curves really do flatten at room temperature at the very end, so any flat section is read as the end of the cooling process. A flat section part-way down a cooling curve is a change of state, such as freezing, at a fixed temperature. Energy continues to leave the substance throughout. The temperature then falls again once the change of state is complete.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Physics (8463) specification; section 4.3.2 Internal energy and energy transfers
